data.why: A long flatbed truck on an open road, seen from a little above so every wheel's angle reads, with an orange post at the corner. Its trip (corner, highway, rear axle, wheel wells, night road, wet road, parking spot, reversing) brings one problem after another: a rod, a computer, a motor, a spring, a 10 degree limit, swivelling headlights, one-wheel braking, crab-walk parking, an angle screen and mirrors. At the end it pivots tight round the same post it flattened at the start. High shots on the axles for each wheel change, the whole truck for each swing.

story.title: How Four-Wheel Steering Turns a Giant Car Like a Compact

recurring.what: the orange post on the corner: flattened by the tail at the start, circled cleanly at the end

ideas.idea: If you steer only the front wheels, you have a wide turn
its long tail swings out and flattens a post
you link a rod that turns the rear wheels
This is four-wheel steering
on the highway, the turned rear wheels whip the tail
a computer turns them the same way above 37 miles per hour
its tiny signal cannot shove the wheels; they sit
an electric motor pushes the rod
if the motor fails, the rod snaps; it veers
a spring pulls the rear wheels straight
turned too far, the rear wheels scrape the body
you limit them to about 10 degrees
at night, 10 degrees of turn leaves the curve dark
the headlights swivel into the turn
in rain, the swiveling lights show the tail skidding
the computer brakes one rear wheel to straighten it
parking, the braked giant swings wide of the spot
at a crawl, all four wheels turn alike, and it slides diagonally
sliding diagonally, the rear wheels turn unseen
a screen shows the driver the rear wheel angle
reversing by screen alone, the tail rolls toward the post
you add mirrors that show the tail
Steer the front wheels, and it circles the post like a compact
Congratulations, you built a giant that turns tight

chain.shows: the tail swings out and flattens the post
at speed the tail whips round
the rear wheels fall back straight and sit
the rod snaps and the truck veers
sparks where the rear wheels scrape the body
the headlights light the road ahead while the turn stays dark
chain.stakes: the driver cannot see the curve

chain.shows: the tail skids out on the wet road
chain.stakes: the truck slides off the road

chain.shows: the truck swings wide past the parking spot
the rear wheels turn where the driver cannot see them
chain.stakes: the driver does not know where the tail goes

chain.shows: the tail rolls back toward the post

surprises.claim: On the Mercedes S-Class, the rear wheels turn opposite the front below about 60 km/h (37 mph) and the same way above that
surprises.search: Mercedes S-Class rear wheel steering 60 km/h same direction

surprises.claim: Mercedes S-Class rear-axle steering turns the rear wheels up to 10 degrees and cuts the turning circle by up to about 2 meters
surprises.search: Mercedes S-Class rear axle steering 10 degrees turning circle 2 meters

surprises.claim: Rear-wheel steering systems use an electric motor actuator on the rear axle to turn the rear wheels.
surprises.search: rear wheel steering electric motor actuator rear axle

surprises.claim: The GMC Hummer EV's CrabWalk turns all four wheels the same way at low speed so the truck moves diagonally.
surprises.search: GMC Hummer EV CrabWalk four wheels same direction diagonal low speed

sentences.text: If you steer only the front wheels, you have a wide turn.
But its long tail swings out and flattens a post.
So you link a rod that turns the rear wheels.
This is four-wheel steering.
But on the highway, the turned rear wheels whip the tail.
So a computer turns them the same way above 37 miles per hour.
But its tiny signal cannot shove the wheels; they sit.
So an electric motor pushes the rod.
But if the motor fails, the rod snaps; it veers.
So a spring pulls the rear wheels straight.
But turned too far, the rear wheels scrape the body.
So you limit them to about 10 degrees.
But at night, 10 degrees of turn leaves the curve dark.
So the headlights swivel into the turn.
But in rain, the swiveling lights show the tail skidding.
So the computer brakes one rear wheel to straighten it.
But parking, the braked giant swings wide of the spot.
So at a crawl, all four wheels turn alike, and it slides diagonally.
But sliding diagonally, the rear wheels turn unseen.
So a screen shows the driver the rear wheel angle.
But reversing by screen alone, the tail rolls toward the post.
So you add mirrors that show the tail.
Steer the front wheels, and it circles the post like a compact.
Congratulations, you built a giant that turns tight.
